Antonelli can be one of the greats and has nothing to prove, says Wolff

MEXICO CITY: Formula One's youngest champion Kimi Antonelli has nothing to prove and could be one of the greats, according to his Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff. The 20-year-old clinched the title in Mexico City on Sunday (Nov 1) to also become the first Italian F1 world champion in 73 years. Wolff, whose team took Britain's Lewis Hamilton to six of his seven championships and also Germany's Nico Rosberg to the crown in 2016, told Reuters Antonelli had exceeded all expectations and was likely to take more titles in years to come. "If we provide him a car in the future then he's not going to be a one-hit wonder," said the Austrian ahead of Sunday's race.

"And if someone else provides him with a car in the future, and we are not able, then he's going to win. "He has all the ingredients of putting himself in a league with the great ones." FERRARI INTEREST NOT A CONCERN  Wolff said he was not worried about any rising clamour in Italy for Ferrari, the sport's most successful and historic team but without a title of any sort since 2008, to try and sign his driver. "Fair enough as a question, no?" he said, speaking in his paddock office. "You can imagine that for a young Italian, in a Ferrari, that might be a topic one day. But the truth is, he knows and appreciates so much the role we played in the past. When we picked him up from 11, how we supported him. There is so much recognition and appreciation for having been with us. "I think we have a very long contract with him. I would have no doubt of him driving for us even without a contract. Even with a car that wouldn't be able to win championships, because he has that appreciation with what we've achieved together. "Now, will there be in the future an interest to drive for Ferrari? Maybe there will be, but you just need to recognise." Antonelli had a difficult debut season in 2025, with Wolff saying he had faced quite a backlash from other drivers and their managers over his decision to bring in someone so young.

Related:

Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion at 20 years old

He recalled some saying it was a joke for such a seemingly raw rookie to go straight into a top team, with others "bombarding" him with messages saying it was reckless and irresponsible and Antonelli needed another year in Formula Two. "And then I heard that all year long last year: 'You saw it was a mistake. He's too young. He's too up and down.'" None of the critics had apologised, said the Austrian. NOTHING TO PROVE Antonelli has won nine races, including five in a row. He triumphed at his home Italian Grand Prix by coming from the back of the field and also stood on top of the podium in Monaco and Spa, two of the classics any driver yearns to have on their resume. Wolff said none of this should have come as a surprise to those who had seen what Antonelli did in the junior series or were aware of how much nurturing and preparation Mercedes had done over the past nine years, spending millions along the way. "This kid has nothing to prove any more," Wolff said, listing Antonelli's domination in karting and titles in single-seaters.  "He has nothing to prove any more because he's proven the last eight years that he's been the best." The Austrian said champions like Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen recognised immediately the arrival of a new talent and threat. "When you see the interaction between Max and Kimi, and Lewis and Kimi, it's always like 'game recognises game'," he added. "From the first time Kimi came on track, Max recognised. And they see it by following. You can see it's different." Wolff said he also had no worries that Antonelli's head might be turned by fame and fortune or by wanting to enjoy the fruits of his success. "We have a good structure around him," he said. "We've built a wall around him. His family, he has all the right values. He has the right mentors around. I think we're shielding him against possible influences.  "You know, he finds it quite astonishing that people ask for autographs or selfies. He's like 'Really? Is that happening to me?' So I don't think he's at risk of becoming the kind of flamboyant young superstar. It's not going to happen."

Source: Reuters/fh

Ukraine evacuates civilians from parts of Kherson region as expiry of Oleshky ceasefire nears

The Oleshky ceasefire is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

St. Andrew's Cathedral in Russian-occupied Nova Kakhovka, is seen across the Dnipro River from the village of Kozatske, during a localised ceasefire linked to a humanitarian aid mission to Oleshky, Kherson region, Ukraine, on Oct 31, 2026. (Photo: AP/Evgeniy Maloletka)

Ukraine's military said it evacuated 167 people from threatened areas of southern Kherson region on Sunday (Nov 1) as a temporary local ceasefire neared expiry, two days after busloads of residents were brought out of the embattled Russian-held town of Oleshky. A six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo. The ceasefire was due to expire at midnight Moscow time (5am Monday, Singapore time). It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. "Units of civil-military cooperation of the 'South' group of forces, in cooperation with representatives of local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region," Ukraine's General Staff wrote on Telegram.

It said the evacuees included 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance. The governor of Kherson region, Oleksandr Prokudin, urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared. "I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called 'red zones' – areas and settlements near the Dnipro," Prokudin wrote on Telegram. "The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high." In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Russia had a positive view of how the operation was conducted in Oleshky, as well as of the coordination between the two countries' human rights commissioners.

Related:

Russia, Ukraine begin Oleshky ceasefire but keep up strikes elsewhere

The pope said he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing a ceasefire in Oleshky would pave the way for broader peace efforts. Melania Trump, writing on X, said the ceasefire "has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack". On Saturday, starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukraine after a circuitous journey from the area, just a few km (miles) from the front line. They first travelled by bus via Crimea, annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014, to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus from where they continued to Ukraine. Those wishing to leave Oleshky - some for Russia, some for Ukraine - were taken initially to Crimea in 25 buses and nine ambulances, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said, before splitting into separate convoys. It was not known how many chose to stay in Russian-held Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River opposite the region's Ukrainian-held main town of Kherson.

Vadym, a Ukrainian sergeant of the 42nd Marine Brigade walks through an area contaminated with anti-personnel mines in front of destroyed houses during an evacuation of local population to a safe area amid a local ceasefire linked to a humanitarian aid mission in Oleshky, in the village of Kozatske, Kherson region, Ukraine, Oct 31, 2026. (Photo: AP/Evgeniy Maloletka)

CEASEFIRE HOLDING The ceasefire has been holding since Tuesday without violations, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials. It has allowed them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town. Russian forces took control of the town immediately after the Feb 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but Ukrainian troops recaptured much of the region, including the town of Kherson, later that year. Military action continued in other parts of Ukraine on Sunday. Regional governors and emergency services reported one death in a strike in the Sumy region on the Russian border, a frequent target, and at least one in the central region of Vinnytsia.

Source: Reuters/fs

Iran ian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday (Nov 1) for a third consecutive day of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran , an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters. The talks come amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after the Nov 3 US midterm elections. President Donald Trump has said the United States will not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action afterwards. Iran 's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran is prepared for "both defence and diplomacy". Speaking to state media, Araqchi said discussions on a "two-day proposal" were continuing, but that no final conclusion had been reached.

Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries, as the eight-month-old war continues to disrupt global oil supplies and spill over across the Middle East. "We are doing our best in this process, and we hope that there is rationality on the other side so that they prioritise diplomacy over other paths," Araqchi said of the talks with Qatari officials. Iran 's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday ordered the armed forces to be prepared for any attack, while the military later announced steps to strengthen its readiness. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran , but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically. Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday for discussions with Iran ian officials before moving the talks to Doha on Saturday, an official had told Reuters. The talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington, the official added.

Source: Reuters/fs

WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE: US President Donald Trump returns to the campaign trail on Sunday (Nov 1) with rallies in Iowa and Kansas, Republican-leaning Farm Belt states where his party is fighting to hold US Senate seats, two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress . Trump, who spent Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida after weeks of campaigning across multiple states, won Iowa by double digits in 2024. But polls show Democrats tied with or leading Republicans in many of the state's races. And Trump's approval among rural Americans fell to a new low of 45 percent in October, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, is also facing an unexpectedly close race. Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers.

Democrats and many Republicans have framed the election as a referendum on Trump's policies. "His agenda, without any question, is on the ballot," Senator Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican, told NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday. Scott, the head of the Republican Senate campaign committee, predicted his party would keep its majority in the chamber. If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they could block Trump's legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities. The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump's agenda without the aid of Congress.

FRANKFURT/PEISSENBERG: German ministers threatened tough penalties for looters and rioters who damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in Frankfurt overnight, while praising security forces for preventing wider violence. Frankfurt emerged as the main flashpoint on Saturday (Oct 31) after tens of thousands of people rallied in dozens of German cities to demand better education and lower living costs in protests organised by campaign group "Gen Z regelt" — "Gen Z takes charge". In the financial hub Frankfurt, hooded rioters damaged 17 stores, of which five were looted, Roman Poseck, interior minister of the state of Hesse, told a press conference on Sunday. He said police deployed 1,300 officers, with more than 100 injured in clashes. Police arrested 54 people aged between 13 and 29.

"I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: Things cannot go on like this," Poseck said. Poseck said most of those arrested were German nationals, adding that many of those involved in the disturbances were of an immigrant background, citing information from the police. "Police currently estimate that they are dealing with between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from an immigrant background," he added.

PROTESTERS THROW PETROL BOMBS AT POLICE Frankfurt police reported violent disturbances including windows being smashed and petrol bombs, rocks and bottles being thrown at the emergency services. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, said perpetrators would be identified and held to account. "I expect there to be severe penalties. We are not prepared to accept, in the slightest, that such incidents and such rioting should take place here," he told reporters on Sunday. He accused "troublemakers from the immigrant community" of acting alongside left-wing extremists and other far-left groups, but did not provide evidence to support the claim or say which groups had joined the demonstrations. Dobrindt said a policing strategy based on a large security presence and deployments across multiple locations had proved effective. In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses. Dobrindt said that border controls had been tightened ahead of the protests out of fear extremist groups from abroad could exploit them to stir riots.

Source: Reuters/fs

SOFIA: Bulgarians went to the polls on Sunday (Nov 1) to elect a president after a tight race between the two leading candidates failed to produce an outright winner in last weekend's first round vote for the largely ceremonial role. Incumbent president, Iliana Iotova, 61, led over ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, but fell short of the 50 per cent threshold in the first round race of 27 candidates that saw a record-low turnout. Exit polls will be published after voting ends at 8 pm (1800 GMT), with a result likely on Monday as the ballot papers are counted. The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.

About two dozen seafarers are feared dead and the strikes have prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security. On Wednesday a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones. Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes' outcome "benefits the Russian Federation". They have both called for a diplomatic end to the war. A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president. She became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter and win a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier. A host of right-leaning political figures, among them ex-premier Boiko Borisov, have expressed support for Gyurov.
